explanations.explanation: Compassion, friend. Isaiah says, “For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob…” before anything else happens. The very first thing Jacob gets is the LORD's tenderness. Everything after that, the choosing and the homeland, grows out of it.

I get why you'd guess that, since this song gets sharp later on. But verse 1 starts softer. Isaiah says the LORD will have compassion on Jacob. The sharp words are saved for Babylon's king, and Jacob gets a homeland.

Anger does show up in this passage, but it belongs to the oppressor. The staff of the wicked “struck the peoples in anger…” (Isaiah 14:6). Toward Jacob, verse 1 says the LORD will have compassion. Different word, very different morning.
True. Isaiah says, “once again He will choose Israel and settle them in their own land.” Hear that "once again"? It's a fresh start for Israel. The LORD isn't done with them.

Verse 1 actually says the opposite. The LORD will choose Israel "once again" and settle them in their own land. Isaiah's words are “once again He will choose Israel…” That's a second chance, friend, not a goodbye.

I can see why that sounds natural, but the text goes the other way. Isaiah says, “The foreigner will join them and unite with the house of Jacob.” So the foreigner isn't kept away. They come in and join up. The more the merrier, like a second tray of cookies nobody saw coming.

False is right, baker. Isaiah says, “The foreigner will join them and unite with the house of Jacob.” Nobody is shown the door in this verse. The foreigner joins up and stands with the house of Jacob.
That's it. Isaiah says, “They will make captives of their captors and rule over their oppressors.” The ones who held Israel are the ones held. Quite the turnaround, friend.

Silver is a fair guess, since paying someone back is a real thing people do. But Isaiah never mentions silver here. He says Israel will “make captives of their captors and rule over their oppressors.” That's a whole different kind of payback.
Sending them away sounds like a clean ending, but that's not what the verse says. Isaiah says Israel “will make captives of their captors…” The captors don't leave. They end up held themselves.

Contempt is right. Isaiah says, “you will sing this song of contempt against the king of Babylon.” It's not a gentle tune. It's aimed straight at the king, and it's a song for the day the LORD gives rest.
Mourning is a decent guess, because a king falling feels like something people might grieve. But Isaiah calls this “a song of contempt.” It's sung against the king of Babylon, not for him.

Thanks fits the mood, since the day is about rest after hard labor. But the verse names the song itself. Isaiah says, “you will sing this song of contempt against the king of Babylon.” So the word is contempt, friend.
The LORD, friend. The song says, “The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers.” No army gets the credit. The One who broke it is the One who gave rest.
Pharaoh, Egypt's king, is a name people know, so it's an easy one to grab. But he isn't in this song. The song says, “The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked…” Look to the LORD for this one.

The king of Assyria sounds like a powerful candidate, but this song never names him. It says, “The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers.” So the answer is the LORD. Nobody else gets the credit.
Rage is right. The staff of the wicked “subdued the nations in rage with relentless persecution.” That's how the oppressor ruled before the LORD broke it. Relentless, rage, no breaks.
I wish it were mercy. But the song says, “it subdued the nations in rage with relentless persecution.” Mercy is nowhere in that line. It shows what the LORD broke.
Wisdom would have made for a different song, friend. The verse says, “it subdued the nations in rage with relentless persecution.” That rage is what the song is looking back on. The LORD broke it.

It's easy to see why you'd think that, but the earth doesn't weep here. Isaiah says, “All the earth is at peace and at rest; they break out in song.” So it's singing, not crying. Nobody's reaching for tissues in this verse.
False is right. The song says, “All the earth is at peace and at rest; they break out in song.” Peace and rest come first, and then the singing starts. The whole earth sounds relieved.

That's it. The trees say, “Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us.” They have their own reason to sing. Trees who don't have to worry about the woodcutter are trees in a good mood, friend.

explanations.answer: The rain has finally come back
explanations.explanation: Rain would make a tree happy, I'll give you that. But the song gives a different reason. The trees say, “Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us.” It's all about the woodcutter.

explanations.answer: Their roots have room to grow
explanations.explanation: Roots with room sounds like a nice life for a tree. But the cedars and cypresses say it themselves: “Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us.” That's the whole reason they sing.

The rulers of the earth, that's right. Sheol “stirs the spirits of the dead to greet you,” and these are all the rulers of the earth. Every one of those kings gets the news that someone new is arriving.

I see why prophets came to mind, since Isaiah is one. But the verse names a different group. Sheol stirs up the spirits of the dead, and they are all the rulers of the earth. The prophets aren't mentioned here.
Angels make sense if you're thinking of a big welcome. But the song says Sheol is below, and it stirs up the spirits of the dead. They're all the rulers of the earth. No angels are in this scene.

Seated is a fair guess for kings, since thrones are made for sitting. But the verse says Sheol “makes all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones.” So they stand up. Even kings get up when the king of Babylon comes in.
False is right. Sheol “makes all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones.” They don't stay put. They get up to meet him.

explanations.answer: You have become weak like us
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. The dead kings tell him, “You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!” The king who made nations tremble is now one of them. Funny how a throne doesn't come with a warranty.

explanations.answer: You will rule over us here
explanations.explanation: A ruler taking over sounds like how a king might think. But the kings in Sheol don't hand him anything. They say, “You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!” He's weak like them, with no crown to rule from.

explanations.answer: You are stronger than us all
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a welcome he'd have wanted. But the dead kings tell him, “You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!” Strong is the last word they use. They call him weak.
Destroyer, yes. The song says, “You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations.” That's the name the song gives him. Cut down, that's how it ends.
Defender would be a kinder title. But the song says, “You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations.” The nations weren't defended by him. He's called their destroyer.
A shepherd looks after the sheep, so the word does sound nicer. But the song calls him a “destroyer of nations.” Nobody gets looked after in this verse. The word is destroyer.
Throne is it. He says in his heart, “I will raise my throne above the stars of God.” A throne above the stars. That's one tall chair.

A banner is a fair guess, since rulers like to wave something. But he says in his heart, “I will raise my throne above the stars of God.” It's his throne he wants raised, and that tells you what he's after.
An altar would make it a different kind of plan. The king says in his heart, “I will raise my throne above the stars of God.” It's a throne he wants, not an altar. He's got a seat on his mind.

explanations.answer: To make himself like the Most High
explanations.explanation: That's the last "I will." He says, “I will make myself like the Most High.” The Most High is God. Look at how high those wishes climbed, and you see why the song pulls him down.

explanations.answer: To make peace with every nation
explanations.explanation: Peace would be a good ending, but it isn't his. The song has him say, “I will make myself like the Most High.” Every "I will" is about himself, and this last one reaches highest.

explanations.answer: To build a temple for the LORD
explanations.explanation: Building a temple would be a humble plan. But his last words are, “I will make myself like the Most High.” He isn't building anything for the LORD. He's reaching for the LORD's place.

explanations.answer: The lowest depths of the Pit
explanations.explanation: The lowest depths of the Pit, that's right. The song says, “But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit.” He wanted to go up above the clouds. The song sends him the other direction.
The sea is deep, so I see where that comes from. But the song doesn't say sea anywhere. It says he will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit.

Valley of Hinnom is a real place name, but this song never mentions it. The song says, “But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit.” That's where he ends up. He was aiming up, and the song says down.

explanations.answer: Is this the man who shook the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the question. Those who see him ask, “Is this the man who shook the earth…” They can hardly believe it's the same guy. He made kingdoms tremble, and now people just stare.

explanations.answer: Is this the man who healed the land
explanations.explanation: Healed is the opposite of what they remember. The people ask, “Is this the man who shook the earth and made the kingdoms tremble,” and they don't ask about healing. The next verse says he turned the world into a desert.

explanations.answer: Is this the man who built our cities
explanations.explanation: Building sounds like a ruler's proud résumé. But the people stare and ask, “Is this the man who shook the earth…” The song says he destroyed cities (Isaiah 14:17). So building isn't what they remember.

I can see why you'd think that, but it's the opposite. The people remember him as the one “who refused to let the captives return to their homes.” So he's remembered for keeping captives. Letting them go isn't in that line.
False, and that's the right call. The people remember him as the one “who refused to let the captives return to their homes.” He said no to letting them go home. That's the memory that sticks.

explanations.answer: He is cast out of his grave
explanations.explanation: That's what the song says. “But you are cast out of your grave like a rejected branch…” The other kings are resting in their tombs, and he isn't. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the song.

explanations.answer: He is buried with great honor
explanations.explanation: Great honor is how kings are usually remembered. But the song says, “But you are cast out of your grave like a rejected branch…” That "But" separates him from the other kings. It's a heavy verse, so no honor here.

explanations.answer: He is laid among his fathers
explanations.explanation: That's how some kings are laid to rest, but not this one. The song says, “But you are cast out of your grave like a rejected branch…” The word "But" marks the difference. I think this part is heavy.

explanations.answer: He destroyed his land and slaughtered his people
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the song gives. “You will not join them in burial, since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people.” It's heavy to read, and I think it is meant to be. The reason is what he did to his own land and people.

explanations.answer: He never built a tomb for himself
explanations.explanation: A missing tomb would be a simple reason. But the song gives a different one: “since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people.” That's a heavy line, and it names why. A tomb isn't the point.

explanations.answer: His own sons refused to bury him
explanations.explanation: That's an easy thing to imagine, but the song never says it. It gives this reason: “since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people.” It's a heavy line. His sons aren't named as the reason.

I can see why you'd think that, but it's the opposite. The song says, “They will never rise up to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities.” That's a hard line to read, and it says no. His sons don't rise up.
False is right. The song says, “They will never rise up to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities.” It's a heavy verse. The text says "never," so no land and no cities for them.

True. The LORD says, “I will cut off from Babylon her name and her remnant, her offspring and her posterity,” declares the LORD. Four things are named, and He says He will cut them all off. That's the LORD speaking in His own voice.

It's the other way around. The LORD says, “I will cut off from Babylon her name and her remnant, her offspring and her posterity,” declares the LORD. Name, remnant, offspring, all named. The LORD says it Himself.

Broom, friend. The LORD says, “I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction.” I know a broom. I use one after every batch to chase the crumbs. This one belongs to the LORD, though, and the word is destruction.
A sword feels like the natural pick for a heavy verse. But the LORD says, “I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction.” It's a broom, not a sword. That word "sweep" gives it away.
Fire is a common way to picture an ending, so I get it. But the LORD says, “I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction.” The tool is a broom. Fire isn't in the verse.
